# One Arrow, Not Two

*SN 36.6, the Salla Sutta — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 5 min · 783 words</p>

## Before you read

<div class="reader-guide" markdown="1">

### What happens

The Buddha asks a group of monks what makes the difference between an untrained person and a trained disciple when both experience pleasant, painful, and mixed feelings.

### Central question

When pain is unavoidable, what makes it become an added layer of mental suffering?

### Main point

Both people feel physical pain. The untrained response adds grief and resistance and turns to sensual pleasure for relief. The trained response feels the pain without adding that second mental layer. It understands how feelings arise and pass, what is appealing about them, what danger they carry, and the way out.

### Reading tip

Read the Two Arrows and One Arrow sections as parallel descriptions. Nearly every reaction in the first is answered by its absence in the second.

### This text is not saying

The text does not say that training prevents bodily pain. Its contrast is between pain itself and the mental reaction added to it.

### Key words

<p class="reader-guide__terms-intro">These definitions are here so you do not need to know Pali or Buddhist vocabulary before reading.</p>
<dl class="reader-guide__terms">
<dt><dfn>ordinary person</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;puthujjana&quot; -- someone who has not yet had the breakthrough into the path. It is the standard term for the untrained starting point, not an insult.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble disciple</dfn></dt>
<dd>Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.</dd>
<dt><dfn>resistance</dfn></dt>
<dd>A reflexive pushing-away from what&#x27;s unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.</dd>
<dt><dfn>underlying tendency</dfn></dt>
<dd>A reactive pattern that isn&#x27;t necessarily active right now but is ready to reassert itself given the right conditions -- lying underneath rather than gone.</dd>
<dt><dfn>mixed feeling</dfn></dt>
<dd>A felt experience that is neither clearly pleasant nor clearly unpleasant. Rendered &quot;mixed&quot; rather than &quot;neutral&quot; to keep it an active third register rather than a flat absence of feeling.</dd>
</dl>

</div>

## Translation

### The Difference

"Bhikkhus, an unlearned ordinary person feels pleasant, painful, and mixed
feelings.

A learned noble disciple feels pleasant, painful, and mixed feelings too.

So what's the difference, bhikkhus? What sets them apart?"

"Bhante, our teachings come from the Buddha. The Buddha is our guide, and we
rely on him. Please explain what this means. We will listen and remember it."

"Then listen carefully and pay close attention. I will speak."

"Yes, Bhante," the bhikkhus replied.

The Buddha said this:

### Two Arrows

"Bhikkhus, when an unlearned ordinary person is touched by painful feeling,
they grieve, they wear themselves out, they wail, they beat their chest and
cry, and they lose their bearings.

They feel it twice: once in the body and once in the mind.

Suppose, bhikkhus, someone is shot with an arrow. Then they are shot again
with a second arrow. They would feel both arrows.

It is the same for an unlearned ordinary person. When painful feeling touches
them, they grieve, they wear themselves out, they wail, they beat their chest
and cry, and they lose their bearings.

They feel it twice: once in the body and once in the mind.

When that same painful feeling touches them, they resist it. The underlying
tendency toward resistance in painful feeling remains.

When painful feeling touches them, they turn to sensual pleasure.

Why?

Because sensual pleasure is the only escape from painful feeling they know.
When they delight in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency toward passion
in pleasant feeling remains.

They do not understand those feelings as they have come to be: how they arise
and vanish, what is gratifying about them, what danger they hold, and what
escape there is from them. Because they do not understand all this, the
underlying tendency toward ignorance in mixed feeling remains.

If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it while bound. If they feel a
painful feeling, they feel it while bound. If they feel a mixed feeling, they
feel it while bound.

Bhikkhus, this is what it means to call someone an unlearned ordinary person.
They are bound to birth, ageing, and death. They are bound to sorrow,
lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. I say they are bound to
dissatisfaction."

### One Arrow

"But when a learned noble disciple is touched by painful feeling, bhikkhus,
they do not grieve, they do not wear themselves out, they do not wail, they do
not beat their chest and cry, and they do not lose their bearings.

They feel it once: in the body, not in the mind.

Suppose, bhikkhus, someone is shot with an arrow but not with a second arrow.
They would feel only one arrow.

It is the same for a learned noble disciple. When painful feeling touches
them, they do not grieve, do not wear themselves out, do not wail, do not beat
their chest and cry, and do not lose their bearings.

They feel it once: in the body, not in the mind.

When that same painful feeling touches them, they do not resist it. No
underlying tendency toward resistance in painful feeling remains.

When painful feeling touches them, they do not turn to sensual pleasure.

Why?

Because they know an escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure.
Since they do not delight in sensual pleasure, no underlying tendency toward
passion in pleasant feeling remains.

They understand those feelings as they have come to be: how they arise and
vanish, what is gratifying about them, what danger they hold, and what escape
there is from them. Because they understand all this, no underlying tendency
toward ignorance in mixed feeling remains.

If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it while unbound. If they feel a
painful feeling, they feel it while unbound. If they feel a mixed feeling,
they feel it while unbound.

Bhikkhus, this is what it means to call someone a learned noble disciple.
They are unbound from birth, ageing, and death. They are unbound from sorrow,
lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. I say they are unbound from
dissatisfaction.

That, bhikkhus, is the difference. That is what sets a learned noble disciple
apart from an unlearned ordinary person."

### Verses

"Someone wise and learned
does not add another feeling
to what is pleasant or painful.

This is the great difference
between the steady, skillful person
and the ordinary person.

The learned person has understood the teaching
and sees this world and the next.
Desirable things do not churn their heart,
and undesirable things bring up no resistance.

Favoring and opposing
have been blown away.
They are finished. They are gone.

That person knows the dustless,
sorrowless state.
They have gone beyond becoming
and discern rightly."

The sixth discourse is finished.

<details class="reader-terms">
<summary>Words used in this translation (16)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>arrow</dfn></dt>
<dd>A recurring image across these texts with more than one meaning. In MN 63 it&#x27;s a poisoned arrow -- refusing treatment until every background fact about the wound is known first, a warning against blocking practice with unanswerable questions. In SN 36.6 it&#x27;s a different image entirely: an ordinary person&#x27;s pain is one arrow, and the extra suffering added on top of it is a second, avoidable arrow.</dd>
<dt><dfn>becoming</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;bhava&quot; -- the settling of experience into a way of being that feels like somebody being something. Often translated &quot;existence.&quot;</dd>
<dt><dfn>Bhante</dfn></dt>
<dd>A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly &quot;venerable sir.&quot; Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>birth</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;jāti&quot; -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.</dd>
<dt><dfn>body</dfn></dt>
<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dissatisfaction</dfn></dt>
<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>escape</dfn></dt>
<dd>A genuine way out of being stuck in a feeling -- as opposed to the false escapes (like chasing pleasure) an untrained mind tends to reach for instead.</dd>
<dt><dfn>heart</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;citta&quot; -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the &quot;heart-mind&quot; or &quot;feeling mind&quot;; here &quot;heart&quot; does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ignorance</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;avijjā&quot; -- not general stupidity, but specifically not seeing how dissatisfaction works and how it ends. The first link in the dependent-arising sequence.</dd>
<dt><dfn>mixed feeling</dfn></dt>
<dd>A felt experience that is neither clearly pleasant nor clearly unpleasant. Rendered &quot;mixed&quot; rather than &quot;neutral&quot; to keep it an active third register rather than a flat absence of feeling.</dd>
<dt><dfn>noble disciple</dfn></dt>
<dd>Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.</dd>
<dt><dfn>ordinary person</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;puthujjana&quot; -- someone who has not yet had the breakthrough into the path. It is the standard term for the untrained starting point, not an insult.</dd>
<dt><dfn>resistance</dfn></dt>
<dd>A reflexive pushing-away from what&#x27;s unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.</dd>
<dt><dfn>underlying tendency</dfn></dt>
<dd>A reactive pattern that isn&#x27;t necessarily active right now but is ready to reassert itself given the right conditions -- lying underneath rather than gone.</dd>
<dt><dfn>world</dfn></dt>
<dd>A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world built through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense is meant.</dd>
</dl>
</details>

*[arrow]: A recurring image across these texts with more than one meaning. In MN 63 it's a poisoned arrow -- refusing treatment until every background fact about the wound is known first, a warning against blocking practice with unanswerable questions. In SN 36.6 it's a different image entirely: an ordinary person's pain is one arrow, and the extra suffering added on top of it is a second, avoidable arrow.
*[becoming]: This project's rendering of "bhava" -- the settling of experience into a way of being that feels like somebody being something. Often translated "existence."
*[Bhante]: A respectful way of addressing a senior monastic, roughly "venerable sir." Left untranslated because English has no natural equivalent.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[birth]: This project's rendering of "jāti" -- being born, and the link that ageing and dying depend on in the dependent-arising sequence. In MN 141 the word appears once in its everyday sense instead, in a simile about a mother.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[dissatisfaction]: This translation's rendering of "dukkha," the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated "suffering," but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.
*[escape]: A genuine way out of being stuck in a feeling -- as opposed to the false escapes (like chasing pleasure) an untrained mind tends to reach for instead.
*[heart]: This project's rendering of "citta" -- the affective or feeling side of mind: the part that takes on a mood, wants, leans, reacts, and can be gladdened, steadied, trained, and released. It is sometimes called the "heart-mind" or "feeling mind"; here "heart" does not mean merely emotion or the physical organ.
*[ignorance]: This project's rendering of "avijjā" -- not general stupidity, but specifically not seeing how dissatisfaction works and how it ends. The first link in the dependent-arising sequence.
*[mixed feeling]: A felt experience that is neither clearly pleasant nor clearly unpleasant. Rendered "mixed" rather than "neutral" to keep it an active third register rather than a flat absence of feeling.
*[noble disciple]: Someone who has had the breakthrough into the path and so is no longer merely an ordinary person. It does not mean noble by birth, and does not require being a monastic.
*[ordinary person]: This project's rendering of "puthujjana" -- someone who has not yet had the breakthrough into the path. It is the standard term for the untrained starting point, not an insult.
*[resistance]: A reflexive pushing-away from what's unwanted, arising automatically in response to unpleasant feeling.
*[underlying tendency]: A reactive pattern that isn't necessarily active right now but is ready to reassert itself given the right conditions -- lying underneath rather than gone.
*[world]: A word whose scope shifts with the teaching. It can mean the lived world built through the senses and the mind, or the wider physical cosmos. The surrounding passage shows which sense is meant.
